newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine farm growth brightens economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Philippine farm growth brightens economic outlook.

text.p: Robust Philippine agricultural growth in the first quarter has fuelled hopes the economy remains healthy even as worries continued to hound the stock market the country may become another Thailand, analysts said on Wednesday.
The vital agriculture sector grew 4.22 percent in the first three months, up from 2.49 percent a year earlier, according to the the Bureau of Agricultural Statistics.

It is even more impressive compared to adjusted figures issued by another government office, the National Economic Development Authority, which said a year earlier the sector had contracted 3.04 percent.
The rise gave a much-needed boost to the local stock market which had sunk to 17-month lows on fears the Philippines was about to copy the problems of Thailand's banking and property sectors.
On Wednesday, the market index recovered 1.58 percent to 2,547.36 points.

"Part of the confidence is brought about by the agricultural growth figure for the first quarter, a good indication that maybe the GNP figure is within target." said Asiamerit Securities analyst Ramon Saulo.
The government is scheduled to release the first quarter economic growth figures next week.
Government estimates put growth this year at seven to eight percent this year versus 6.8 percent last year. Gross domestic product is projected at over six percent compared with 5.5 percent.

The growth in the farm sector, which accounts for 21 percent of economic output compared to 24 percent for manufacturing, is the latest in the list of data attesting to the soundness of the country's economic foundation, economists said.
Last week, the government reported the growth in the first quarter trade deficit slowed to 8.4 percent versus a 41 percent growth a year ago.
"The numbers are good," said Conrad Andres, research head of DBP-Daiwa Securities. "That should offset the slowdown in manufacturing."
The volume of production index fell 1.8 percent year-on-year in the first two months, largely due to declines in garments, transport equipment and paper products.

Andres said he expected gross domestic product in the first quarter to be above five percent, which is in the higher range of the band of 4.8 to 5.2 percent growth forecast the brokerage house made for the period.

"(But) the stock market would like to see the total picture. There is still some concern manufacturing didn't do as well...which was fed by the poor corporate results," said Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securities.
"I still think GNP will still be alright," said Omar Cruz, vice president of Citibank. "Nothing has happened which should affect GNP even if corporate earnings are suffering."
Cruz said the blue chip companies, such as San Miguel Corp, showed dismal earnings because of stiffer competition from imported products.
"The purchasing power is still there. It just shifted to more competitive imported products," Cruz argued."On aggregate, the pie has continued to increase."
"That is the effect of industrial restructuring... the effect of liberalisation," he said, which should eventually force local companies to be more efficient.
